text: Gilgamesh: Once We Know We Will Die, Why Return to Living?
Gilgamesh did not begin to fear death when he first heard of it.
He already lived in a world where people died.

He had seen danger and willingly walked toward it. He and Enkidu journeyed to the Cedar Forest, killed Humbaba, and then together killed the Bull of Heaven. Death had always been beside their path. But then it belonged more to enemies, to adventure, to something that heroic deeds could defeat or postpone.
Until Enkidu died.
Someone who had walked, fought, and talked with him suddenly no longer answered.
Gilgamesh wept and kept vigil beside his friend's body, unable to accept that the change had already happened. Then his fear turned from Enkidu toward himself:
Will I be like this too?
That question added no new piece of knowledge.
It merely brought a long-familiar statement into Gilgamesh's own future for the first time.
Everyone dies.
It turns out that “everyone” includes me.
Facts become something different when they enter our own lives.
You may always have known your parents would grow old, yet truly understand those words only when you see them unable to do something they once did with ease.
You may know a relationship can end, yet discover that “ending” is not an abstract noun only when the other person stops coming back.
You may know your time is limited, yet keep putting everything important off until later, until a loss makes “later” something you can no longer take for granted.
Knowledge answers: what is the world usually like?
Life asks: since this will happen to me too, how am I to go on now?
Enkidu's death turned mortality from part of the world's order into Gilgamesh's own question.
So he left Uruk to seek Utnapishtim, the man said to have gained immortality.
This quest is often understood as the arrogance of a hero unwilling to accept human limits.
But if there really are things in life worth continuing, wanting more time is not absurd.
If love, creation, understanding, and life together have value, why should wishing them not to be cut short automatically be a mistake?
Death frightens us precisely because being alive is not a matter of caring about nothing.
When Gilgamesh finally found Utnapishtim, his first response was bewilderment.
The man before him did not look fundamentally different from himself.
He was neither an incomprehensible god nor an entirely different kind of being.
So Gilgamesh asked:
You are like me. Why were you granted everlasting life?
This is almost a question about fairness.
If no one had ever passed beyond death, death could be understood as a condition without exception.
But once an exception exists, the question becomes: why does this possibility belong to him and not to me?
We often encounter similar imbalances in life.
Others receive opportunities we lack, escape losses we cannot avoid, or have a life that truly exists but is not open to everyone.
“Someone in the world has done it” easily becomes “so if you work hard enough, you can do it too.”
But a possibility that once existed does not thereby become a path anyone can reproduce.
Utnapishtim's immortality came from a unique flood and a decision by the gods.
He could tell his own story, but he could not turn everlasting life into a technique Gilgamesh could acquire simply by learning, persevering, or proving himself.
The exception shows that death is not logically without exception.
Yet it offers Gilgamesh no path he can actually follow through.
This may be crueler than never finding Utnapishtim at all.
For Gilgamesh finally stands before an immortal, only to discover that the man's existence cannot open the same door for him.
Some things people possess are real but cannot be transferred.
Some past miracles can be told, but cannot become a plan for those who come afterward.
This is not fair, and it need not be explained away as fair.
It simply leaves “Why not me?” without an answer that can take away the pain.
Utnapishtim also asks Gilgamesh to try resisting sleep.
Gilgamesh soon falls asleep.
A man who wants to defeat death cannot even will away the interruption of consciousness that recurs in everyday life.
This failure certainly does not simply prove that sleep equals death. With its awakening, sleep belongs to life; death does not send us back to our old relationships and unfinished business.
But the test reveals a more modest fact:
Wanting intensely to go on does not mean we can make our bodies and time obey our wishes without limit.
Desire can determine what we pursue.
It cannot, by itself, determine what the world gives back.
Later, the epic offers Gilgamesh one smaller hope.
He learns of a plant on the seabed that can restore youth to the old. He obtains it, but does not immediately use it alone. He plans to take it back to Uruk and let an old person try it first.
At this point, his quest seems to change.
He no longer wants only to wrest his own immortality from the world; he also wants to bring the possibility of renewal back into shared life.
But on the journey home, a snake steals the plant while he is bathing, then sheds its old skin.
Gilgamesh loses again.
This time, no god steps forward to punish him, and no enemy fights him.
A chance opening is enough for something won through hardship to slip away.
He weeps and asks for whom he has labored.
That question touches the vulnerability of every effort we invest.
We are willing to give something to a task because we believe our effort can become part of its outcome. But the world does not guarantee that those who make the effort will always keep the result.
Time, chance, other people, and our bodies all enter our actions, so that what ultimately happens no longer belongs entirely to the original plan.
This does not make effort meaningless.
Nor does it guarantee that effort will be rewarded.

In an earlier Old Babylonian tablet tradition, the tavern keeper Siduri advises Gilgamesh: the gods gave death to humans and kept life in their own hands; people should therefore eat, wear clean clothes, bathe, and cherish daily life with children and a partner.
This passage later became very famous.
It is easily presented as the epic's final lesson: since you cannot live forever, stop thinking about death and enjoy the life before you.
But this advice belongs to an earlier Old Babylonian textual tradition. It cannot be treated, without marking the difference, as the conclusion at the same point in the Standard Babylonian version.
And even taken on its own, the passage should not be read too lightly.
A meal did not bring Enkidu back.
Clean clothes and family routines did not make the loss disappear.
If “returning to life” means anything, it cannot mean replacing the question of death with small pleasures.
It can only mean this:
Death remains unresolved, but finite life has not thereby lost its right to be life.
That is different from “stop thinking about it.”
Someone who has come to know death cannot truly return to a time before knowing it.
They can only go on carrying that knowledge.
The Standard Babylonian version brings Gilgamesh back to Uruk in a different way.
The epic shows us the city walls again.
This, too, is often interpreted to mean that individuals die, but great works and fame grant another kind of immortality.
There is support for such a reading, but it should not be presented as the only answer.
The walls cannot answer Gilgamesh in Enkidu's place.
Nor can public achievements prevent the builder's own death.
Leaving a work behind and continuing to live oneself are two different things.

A work can enter the world of those who come later, and a person's influence can outlast their life. But to say death has therefore been conquered merely substitutes “still being remembered” for “no longer existing.”
Both matter, but they are not the same.
Gilgamesh's turning back toward Uruk at least shows that his life has reentered the shared human world.
He is no longer only fleeing his own death in the wilderness.
But returning does not mean the question is closed.
He will still die.
Enkidu has still not returned.
The walls are simply something that can continue within these facts.
What, then, does death teach us about how to live?
In fact, it teaches us no answer directly.
“Life is finite” does not entail seizing immediate pleasure, because long-term care, learning, and building all require giving up some pleasures now.
It does not entail pursuing great achievements, because some of the most important lives leave no grand works behind.
It does not entail starting a family, nor withdrawing from every relationship.
It does not entail living each day as if it were the last, because a real lifetime requires commitments to tomorrows that are not the last day.
Death changes the conditions of choice. It does not make our choices for us.
It tells us:
Time cannot be deferred indefinitely.
Choosing one path will gradually close off others.
Some words, if left forever unsaid, may not have an endlessly available next chance.
Some work will be cut short before it is finished.
Some relationships will one day be remembered by only one of the two people.
These facts give choices weight.
But weight is not direction.
A weighty choice can still be wrong. A finite life does not automatically become meaningful merely because it is finite.
This distinction matters because “accepting death” is sometimes used to dress up losses that could have been avoided.
Some say that since everyone dies, we need not ask too insistently whether a particular death could have been prevented.
Some say finitude makes life precious, making efforts to extend life, reduce suffering, or protect safety seem like a rejection of the natural order.
But acknowledging that death cannot be abolished altogether is not the same as accepting that no particular death need be resisted.
Gilgamesh's search for immortality cannot simply be judged a failure to understand life.
He has lost his closest friend. Of course he has reason to refuse to let death have the last word.
The failure of his quest does not, in reverse, prove that death itself is good.
Death can show us that time is not an unlimited resource.
That does not mean death deserves praise.
Limits force action to choose. That does not make every loss those limits cause legitimate.
There is another place Enkidu's death occupies that must not be overlooked.
It is not merely the starting point of Gilgamesh's growth.
If we say only “his friend's death taught the hero that life is finite,” Enkidu becomes, once again, a means for someone else to gain insight.
His death is first of all his own life cut short, a relationship that cannot continue, and a particular loss Gilgamesh cannot make good.
People often learn from others' suffering.
Such learning may genuinely occur, but it cannot settle the account by declaring the suffering “worth it.”
That Enkidu's death changed Gilgamesh does not mean Enkidu ought to have died for that change.
An outcome can produce value while the loss that caused it remains a loss.
Otherwise, every irreparable harm could be rewritten as a necessary lesson because someone later became more mature.
The epic does not ask us to comfort ourselves in this way.
Gilgamesh's mourning is so intense precisely because no insight gained afterward can be equivalent to Enkidu.
Gilgamesh does come back in the end.
Returning is neither admitting defeat nor finally agreeing that “mortals should not think so much.”
He has simply reached the point where the quest truly breaks off.
The exception of immortality cannot be reproduced.
The attempt to resist sleep fails.
The rejuvenating plant is lost too.
Once every route around death has closed, one by one, he must still face a fact these failures have not canceled:
He is still alive.
Being alive is not a complete answer.
It merely makes it possible to keep bearing the question.
As long as today is not over, we can still choose, return to relationships, finish part of a task, or change our earlier direction.
These actions do not become false because death will eventually come.
Nor does their reality abolish death.
The difficulty of finite life lies precisely in both being true at once.
When Gilgamesh set out, he hoped to find a way to go on forever.
When he returned, he had not found it.
But neither had he proved that life should be content with the everyday, or that only walls and fame are worth leaving behind.
The epic is more restrained than those conclusions.
It lets a person pursue immortality all the way to the end, then sends him back into a world where there will still be losses and unfinished things.
Death has not taught him whom to love, what to build, or how to divide his days.
It has only taken away the guarantee of endless postponement.
From now on, what matters cannot wait until later forever.
But what truly matters must still be answered by the living.
Perhaps that is why, once we know we will die, we still have to return to living.
Not because the question of death has been resolved.
But because, as long as we can still return, the answer can still happen only here.

*Textual basis and version note: This essay draws mainly on Tablets VIII–XI of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh: Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh's search for Utnapishtim, the flood and the unique origin of his immortality, the test of resisting sleep, the loss of the rejuvenating plant, and the return to Uruk. Siduri's advice about food, clean clothes, bathing, and daily family life is explicitly introduced as part of the earlier Old Babylonian textual tradition, not silently spliced into the Standard version. Nor does this essay declare “walls or achievements are immortality” to be the epic's only conclusion.*
